blocks.content: FCFS, short for First Come First Served, is the simplest possible way to schedule a CPU. It works exactly the way the name sounds: whoever arrives first gets served first, just like a single line at a shop counter where the person who joined the queue first is served before everyone behind them.

This chapter walks through exactly how FCFS decides who runs next, traces a fully worked example by hand so you can see completion time, turnaround time and waiting time computed step by step, explains the convoy effect that makes FCFS a poor choice on its own, and closes with what interviewers are really testing when they ask about it.
1. What FCFS Means

FCFS is the most basic CPU scheduling algorithm there is. Processes are served strictly in the order they arrive in the ready queue. There is no consideration of how long a process will take, how important it is, or anything else. The only thing that matters is when it showed up.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: FCFS schedules processes in exactly the order they arrive in the ready queue, and once a process starts it runs to completion or until it blocks, with no interruptions.

["The ready queue behaves as a plain first in first out queue, ordered purely by arrival time.","Whichever process has been waiting the longest is the one the scheduler picks next.","FCFS is non preemptive, meaning a running process is never forced off the CPU by the arrival of another process.","If two processes arrive at exactly the same time, ties are usually broken by process id or by the order they were submitted."]
items: The ready queue behaves as a plain first in first out queue, ordered purely by arrival time.
Whichever process has been waiting the longest is the one the scheduler picks next.
FCFS is non preemptive, meaning a running process is never forced off the CPU by the arrival of another process.
If two processes arrive at exactly the same time, ties are usually broken by process id or by the order they were submitted.

blocks.content: 2. Non Preemptive Execution and the Ready Queue
blocks.text: 2. Non Preemptive Execution and the Ready Queue

blocks.content: The word non preemptive is the single most important detail about FCFS, and it is also the detail people forget fastest. Once a process starts running, it keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or voluntarily gives it up by blocking on I/O. No other process, no matter how short its own burst would be, can interrupt it and take over.
Why this matters

Contrast this with a preemptive algorithm, where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst, or a higher priority, can knock the currently running process back into the ready queue. FCFS does none of that. A ten second process that started a moment ago will run for the full ten seconds even if a process needing only a tenth of a second arrives one instant later. The new arrival simply joins the back of the queue and waits.
Arrival order decides who runs next, and once chosen, a process is untouchable until it finishes or blocks. That single rule is the entire algorithm.
3. A Fully Worked Example
Numbers make this concrete. Take three processes P1, P2 and P3, all arriving close together but at different moments, with different amounts of CPU work to do.

Since all three arrival times are different and already increasing, the FCFS order is simply P1, then P2, then P3, the same order they arrived in. The scheduler runs P1 starting at time 0. P1 needs 5 units of CPU time, so it occupies the CPU until time 5. P2 arrived back at time 1, but the CPU was busy with P1 the whole time, so P2 has to wait until time 5 to start, then runs for its 3 unit burst until time 8. P3 arrived at time 2, but again the CPU stays busy with P1 and then P2, so P3 does not get to start until time 8, and its 8 unit burst keeps it running until time 16.

Time:     0        5        8                        16
          |---P1---|---P2---|-----------P3-----------|

P1 runs from 0 to 5   (burst 5)
P2 runs from 5 to 8   (burst 3, waited from arrival at 1 until start at 5)
P3 runs from 8 to 16  (burst 8, waited from arrival at 2 until start at 8)

blocks.content: From this Gantt chart trace, completion time, turnaround time and waiting time for each process follow directly from three simple formulas: completion time is when the process finishes on the CPU, turnaround time is completion time minus arrival time, and waiting time is turnaround time minus burst time.
{"headers":["Process","Arrival Time","Burst Time","Completion Time","Turnaround Time","Waiting Time"],"rows":[["P1","0","5","5","5","0"],["P2","1","3","8","7","4"],["P3","2","8","16","14","6"]]}

Average waiting time works out to (0 plus 4 plus 6) divided by 3, which is about 3.33 units. Average turnaround time works out to (5 plus 7 plus 14) divided by 3, which is about 8.67 units. Notice that P3 has the longest wait of the three even though it is not the process causing the delay, it is simply unlucky enough to be stuck behind two other processes in the queue.
4. The Convoy Effect

The convoy effect is the most famous and most serious flaw in FCFS. It happens whenever a long, CPU bound process happens to land at the front of the ready queue. Every shorter process behind it must sit and wait for the entire long process to finish, even though running those short processes first would have kept the whole system feeling far more responsive.

blocks.title: Why the name convoy
blocks.content: Picture a slow truck stuck at the front of a single lane road. Every car behind it, no matter how fast it could otherwise go, is forced to crawl along at the truck speed until the truck finally turns off. FCFS creates exactly this pattern among processes.

To see the damage this does, extend the example. Suppose P1 arrives with a long CPU bound burst of 24 units, and right behind it P2, P3 and P4 each need only 3 units, with all four processes arriving at time 0. Because FCFS only looks at arrival order, P1 runs first from 0 to 24, and P2, P3 and P4 are left sitting idle in the ready queue for the entire 24 units even though together their total work is only 9 units.

The average waiting time in this FCFS ordering is (0 plus 24 plus 27 plus 30) divided by 4, which comes out to 20.25 units. Now compare that against simply running the three short processes first and the long one last, the order that a burst aware algorithm such as Shortest Job First would choose.
{"headers":["Scheduling order","Average waiting time"],"rows":[["FCFS, arrival order: P1, P2, P3, P4","20.25"],["Shortest burst first: P2, P3, P4, P1","4.5"]]}

Simply reordering the same four processes cuts the average waiting time from 20.25 down to 4.5, a difference of more than four times. This single scenario is exactly why FCFS is rarely used alone in real systems, and it is the classic example used to motivate more sophisticated algorithms like Shortest Job First, covered in the sibling topic on SJF.

5. Advantages of FCFS
Despite its flaws, FCFS earns its place as the starting point for learning about scheduling because of a few genuine strengths.

["Extremely simple to understand and implement, it is little more than a plain queue.","Fair in the narrow sense that arrival order is respected exactly, nobody is ever skipped over based on judgment calls about importance.","No starvation, every process that joins the queue is guaranteed to eventually be served, since the queue only ever moves forward."]
items: Extremely simple to understand and implement, it is little more than a plain queue.
Fair in the narrow sense that arrival order is respected exactly, nobody is ever skipped over based on judgment calls about importance.
No starvation, every process that joins the queue is guaranteed to eventually be served, since the queue only ever moves forward.

blocks.content: 6. Disadvantages of FCFS
The same simplicity that makes FCFS easy to reason about is also what makes it a poor fit for most real workloads.

["Poor average waiting time whenever burst times vary widely across processes, exactly as the worked examples above show.","The convoy effect, where one long process at the front of the queue drags down every shorter process stuck behind it.","Not suitable for interactive or time sharing systems, where users expect quick responses and cannot tolerate waiting behind an unrelated long running job."]
items: Poor average waiting time whenever burst times vary widely across processes, exactly as the worked examples above show.
The convoy effect, where one long process at the front of the queue drags down every shorter process stuck behind it.
Not suitable for interactive or time sharing systems, where users expect quick responses and cannot tolerate waiting behind an unrelated long running job.

blocks.content: 7. Common Mistakes
A few misunderstandings show up again and again when people first learn FCFS, both in coursework and in interviews.
Forgetting that FCFS is non preemptive
blocks.text: Forgetting that FCFS is non preemptive

blocks.content: A currently running process can never be interrupted under FCFS, not even by a much shorter process that arrives a moment later. It is easy to accidentally reason about FCFS as if it were preemptive and let a short job jump ahead, but that is simply not how the algorithm works.
Confusing completion time with turnaround time
blocks.text: Confusing completion time with turnaround time

blocks.content: Completion time is the raw clock time at which a process finishes on the CPU. Turnaround time is completion time minus arrival time, the total time the process spent in the system from the moment it arrived. Waiting time is turnaround time minus burst time, the portion of that total spent waiting rather than actually running. Mixing these three up is the most common arithmetic mistake in a worked Gantt chart example.
8. The Interview Angle

FCFS is a common starting point interview question precisely because tracing through a Gantt chart by hand, arrival times, burst times, completion times, turnaround times and waiting times all lined up, reveals immediately whether a candidate genuinely understands the mechanics or has only memorized the name. An interviewer can also extend the question by asking what happens if a long process arrives first, which is the natural opening to discuss the convoy effect and why algorithms like Shortest Job First and Round Robin exist.

blocks.title: Quick recap to keep ready
blocks.content: FCFS serves processes in arrival order, non preemptive, no interruptions once started. Turnaround time equals completion time minus arrival time. Waiting time equals turnaround time minus burst time. The convoy effect is a long process at the front delaying every short process behind it.
